diagnosis_verifications.diagnosis: NSAID/analgesic‑related acute‑on‑chronic kidney injury (triple‑whammy, possible papillary necrosis)
supporting_evidence_verified: Dilute urine (SG 1.00) with glucosuria and ketonuria indicating proximal tubular leak
Severe CKD (eGFR 15.6) consistent with chronic NSAID nephropathy
evidence_gaps: Exact timing of creatinine rise to confirm acute‑on‑chronic component
Urine microscopy for casts or papillary necrosis signs
Renal imaging (ultrasound/CT) to assess papillary necrosis or obstruction
concerns: Probability was underestimated; this is the dominant explanation for most findings

supporting_evidence_verified: Long‑standing essential hypertension on three agents
evidence_gaps: Renal ultrasound showing small, echogenic kidneys typical of arteriolar disease
concerns: Over‑estimated probability relative to tubular phenotype

diagnosis_verifications.diagnosis: Early diabetic‑type tubular injury / incipient diabetic nephropathy
evidence_gaps: Urine albumin‑to‑creatinine ratio to differentiate albumin‑only proteinuria
Retinal exam or other microvascular diabetic complications
concerns: Findings (glucosuria, ketonuria) better explained by proximal tubular leak from nephrotoxins

evidence_gaps: Abrupt creatinine rise after ACE‑I initiation
concerns: No clinical clues (flash pulmonary edema, refractory hypertension) supporting this

evidence_gaps: Cumulative cisplatin dose and any subsequent nephrotoxic exposures
concerns: Remote exposure makes it unlikely to be the primary driver

supporting_evidence_verified: Very dilute urine could be seen with obstruction
concerns: No symptoms or imaging data to support obstruction

evidence_gaps: Serologic work‑up (ANA, complements, anti‑dsDNA, IgA levels)
concerns: No hematuria or serologic data; probability over‑estimated

diagnosis_verifications.diagnosis: Monoclonal gammopathy / light‑chain deposition disease (AL amyloidosis variant)
evidence_gaps: Serum protein electrophoresis, urine immunofixation, free‑light‑chain assay
concerns: No laboratory evidence provided; probability too high
No data indicating hyperuricemia or crystal deposition

evidence_gaps: ANCA panel, ESR/CRP, chest imaging, sinus evaluation
concerns: No hematuria, pulmonary‑renal syndrome, or ANCA testing
Listed as a differential with a probability; should be recorded as a confirmed fact

diagnosis_verifications.diagnosis: Comorbidity burden (COPD, stage I NSCLC, anemia, NAFLD, obesity‑metabolic syndrome, psychosocial barriers)
supporting_evidence_verified: Documented COPD, NSCLC, anemia, obesity, social issues
concerns: These are contextual modifiers, not competing diagnoses; probability misuse

consistency_checks.detail: Severe CKD labs match CKD‑5 and NSAID‑related tubulointerstitial injury; no contradictions found.
Chronic naproxen plus ACE‑I and thiazide explain acute‑on‑chronic decline and tubular findings.
No diagnosis in the list accounts for leukopenia; requires separate work‑up.
No renal diagnosis explains bilirubin; suggests hepatic or hemolytic process not addressed.

top_concerns: Probabilities assigned to factual items (CKD‑5, comorbidities) are inappropriate.
Leukopenia and urinary bilirubin are unexplained by any listed diagnosis.
Chronic NSAID‑induced tubulointerstitial nephropathy was not listed as a distinct entity.
Low‑probability immune‑complex GN and monoclonal gammopathy are over‑represented.
recommended_primary: Chronic NSAID‑induced tubulointerstitial nephropathy with superimposed acute‑on‑chronic injury (triple‑whammy)
review_summary: The junior differential captured many plausible renal etiologies but mis‑weighted probabilities, omitted the explicit chronic NSAID nephropathy diagnosis, and failed to explain leukopenia and urinary bilirubin. Adjusted probabilities now reflect the dominance of NSAID‑related tubulointerstitial injury, with hypertension as a secondary contributor. Recommendations focus on stopping nephrotoxic agents, completing targeted work‑up for the orphan findings, and initiating CKD‑5 management.
